utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, Teresa McHenry for the Prosecution appearing with Mr. Huber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have the appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Edina Residovic. I appear on behalf of Zejnil Delalic, and my co-counsel is Eugene O'Sullivan from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: My name is Zeljko Olujic, and I appear on behalf of Zdravko Mucic, and co-counsel is Mr. Tomislav Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I am Salih Karabdic from Sarajevo and I appear on behalf Hazim Delic. Co-counsel is Mr. Thomas Moran from Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Cynthia McMurrey, and along with Nancy Boler and Calvin Saunders, we represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, I understand you have some rebuttal evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's hear you. Please swear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may take your seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please state your full name and spell your last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Landy Sparr, S-P-A-R-R.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, are you a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm an MD

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you give us briefly your educational background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received a bachelor of science and history at the University of Wisconsin, a Master in Arts in American Intellectual History at the University of Wisconsin, an MD from the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine. And I did my psychiatry residency at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: As the witness goes through his background, maybe it would be helpful for the Judges to have his CV. May I ask that a copy of his CV be marked. Defence counsel have previously been given copies of this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution document 264.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence has been provided a copy of this before. Unfortunately, I have misplaced mine. I would like to ask if the Prosecution has an extra copy, if I might be provided one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think she will.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recognise Prosecution Exhibit 264 as a copy of your CV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would ask that the doctor's CV be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, how are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm employed by the Veterans Administration in the United States. I'm at the Veterans Administration Hospital in Portland, Oregon. I'm the acting chief of psychiatry there, and I'm the acting clinical director of the mental health division. I'm also an associate professor of psychiatry at Oregon Health Sciences University School of Medicine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In your capacity as acting chief and clinical director, do you supervise a staff? If so, could you just give us an idea of your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's a large mental health division. We have a staff of 150. We treat 6.000 patients. These are veterans. The staff includes nurses, psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers. We have a 30-bed acute psychiatry in-patient unit, a 20-bed substance abuse unit. We have an extensive disability programme, and we have out-patient clinics. We have a PTSD programme, Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. We have a geriatric psychiatry programme. About half of the 6.000 patients, approximately half are Vietnam veterans.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you also engaged in any private practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have my own case load at the VA. I have about a 100 patients. Some of them are Vietnam veterans and some of them have serious problems with PTSD.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you licensed, and if so how are you licensed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm board certified in general psychiatry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you have any certifications or awards as part of your professional career?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm a fellow in the American Psychiatric Association, and I received the distinguished service award from the Oregon Psychiatric Association. That was because of my work in setting up continuing medical education programmes throughout the state. One of the books that I was involved in received the Guttmacher award in 1992 for forensic psychiatry. It received the award as the best book in forensic psychiatry that year.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. The Judges have your CV, so I won't ask you to go through all your publications, but can you give us a brief idea of the amount of publications and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Don't you think we could skip that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's not in issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, as part of your work, does your work undergo peer review and, if so, can you briefly explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have 81 publications. Most of them, probably 90 per cent of them, have been peer reviewed, which means that some people, some colleagues, that the journal designates, they review the work. It can be up to six different reviewers. Also, the talks I've given have essentially been peer reviewed. We have to submit abstracts. The American Psychiatric Association or the American Academy of Psychiatry and Law, if you want to give a talk, you have to submit an abstract, and it's peer reviewed by a committee. It's accepted or rejected based on that peer review. So most of the stuff I do has been peer reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you if have any areas of special interest in your work, but in answering that, I think maybe it would be helpful if you would just focus on the areas that may be relevant to your testimony here today, your areas of special interest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've worked a lot with PTSD and various aspects of it. One thing has been the forensic aspects, also, spiritual aspects of PTSD, the assessment of PTSD in disability cases. One of the first papers I wrote was entitled "Factious PTSD," which essentially had to do with malingering. I've also done a lot of work in the area of victimisation, in America what we call the blame game, where people claim to be victims in order to gain something. I've also done work on the management of violence and violence in a hospital setting and violence against women.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: As part of your professional work, do you have significant experience in the diagnosis of personality disorders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personality disorders were an early interest of mine. I used to teach a course in personality disorders. I've written a couple of things about personality disorders, and because when we evaluate people for disability, we have to decide exactly what their diagnosis is, if they are personality disordered, they do not receive disability. So we've had to develop protocols to evaluate these individuals, and personality disorders is a big aspect of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It's correct, isn't it, that you were contacted by the Office of the Prosecutor in June of this year to help on issues related to the mental health of the accused Esad Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Jim Cowles contacted me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you prepare a report that lists the information that was provided to you, as well as your findings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'm just going to ask, sir, that a copy of that report be shown to you and a copy given to Your Honours. I have an extra copy for Ms. McMurrey if she needs it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I found a copy of that. Thank you, though.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution document 265.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Actually, Ms. McHenry, if I might have another copy. If you are volunteering, I will accept it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise that document, and is it a copy of your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just while we're going through it, I would move into evidence a copy of the doctor's report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted. If the witness recognises it, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, as part of your evaluation, did you travel to The Hague in the early part of July and examine Mr. Esad Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw him on July 6th and 7th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you, both with respect to your examination and any other work you did, just briefly describe what you did as part of your evaluation of Mr. Landzo and the issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I interviewed him for probably about three hours, and I saw him twice. When I saw him, I was focusing on PTSD because that was the issue at the time, but I also had a fairly good sense of his personality. It seems like that might be a short period of time, but when we interview people, in order to get board certified, we're given a half an hour. And in a half an hour, we're supposed to come up with some kind of a sensible diagnosis. So I did have three hours with him, and I went over a number of things with him, including his background. I also talked to him about the indictment against him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In addition to examining Mr. Landzo, is it correct that you examined a number of prior evaluations and examinations conducted by other mental health professionals, as well as some other material which is set out in your report. So I won't bother to go into that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you just please tell the Judges your findings concerning Post Traumatic Stress Syndrome with respect to Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, the diagnosis of PTSD, what you want to find is what they call a biphasic response of avoidance and re-experiencing. This work was developed by Marty Horowitz about 20 years ago. Then they also added the symptoms of increased arousal. It's a cyclic pattern, so people generally avoid and they re-experience that breakthrough re-experience, and then they avoid. It goes up and down like that. They also have symptoms like startle and a lot of physiologic symptoms. He didn't have those. I mean, he was not -- he didn't appear to have PTSD at all. He did not endorse most of the criteria or any of the criteria.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that was my finding now. Then the rest of the evaluation would have to be retrospective.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Judges your opinion concerning whether Mr. Landzo had PTSD in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was difficult, of course, because I wasn't there, but there are some things about his actions in 1992 that you would not expect to see with somebody that had PTSD. The primary problem was he wasn't avoiding. In fact, his actions in '92, some of his actions were about 180 degrees different than somebody that would have PTSD. He was actually anxious to get to the frontlines. I mean, that's what he wanted to do. That's what he told me. That's what he told others. He was trying to get to the frontlines. He was proud to get a rifle and a uniform. If somebody had PTSD, this isn't what they would want to try to do. They would try to avoid. Now, you could say that he couldn't avoid being in the military, but he could have avoided wanting to be on the frontlines. I mean, he could have asked to be a clerk or something like that, but he didn't do that. I don't think he had PTSD. I understand that there was this stressor that he supposedly underwent prior to his experiences in Celebici, and I think it was approximately 10 months prior or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you referring just to the stressor of the training camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the orientation camp. I think that bothered him. I think he got over it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me move forward. Do you have an opinion as to whether or not Mr. Landzo had a personality disorder in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is more difficult. In fact, I'm going to try not to be too provocative here, but every person -- practically every personality trait in the book has been thrown at this guy. I don't think it's that complicated a situation, but I think it's been made relatively complicated. If I could just talk a little bit about personality disorders, personality disorders are actually the -- it's the old idea of neurosis, and they put these disorders on Axis II, they have their own axis, because they are considered non-biologic. So most of your Axis I diagnoses, like affective disorders, schizophrenia, are supposed to be -- most people believe that they are biologic disorders. There is some correlate, genetic correlate. But personality disorders, no. So they have their own axis. Now, we don't really use personality disorders in mitigation. And we don't -- either when we consider disability or generally in the court system, we don't use them in mitigation, and there are two reasons for that. One is that personality disorders --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to object. First of all, he is saying "we don't." Can we be allowed to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Psychiatrists, he means.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: What standard is he applying to that? If he's applying it to a legal system --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When the expert finishes, you will have a right to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm talking about the American system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Your purpose is to cross-examine whatever opinion he has volunteered, not to interrupt his opinion itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most people consider this behaviour volitional. People have control over their personality. And actually the other problem is the diagnosis is difficult to make because the diagnosis has to do with how a person interacts with others. And so if you're talking with somebody or trying to interview them, it's actually more instructive to see them over time and how they interact with other people in non-artificial settings. If somebody is in gaol, it's hard to really see how they interact with others much. So they are difficult to diagnose, but there are criteria developed, and they are rigorous, the criteria, and they are rigorous on purpose. One of the reasons they are rigorous is because when you have a disorder, a personality disorder, you are at the end of the continuum. So you're, like, two standard deviations from the norm. I mean, everybody has these personality traits. Everybody does. There isn't anybody that doesn't have a personality. So these are common traits. I mean, they are traits that everybody shares. So there's a continuum. You get way out on the continuum, then you have a disorder. That's why the criteria are so rigorous. What they did is they clustered these personalities. There are three clusters. One cluster is what they call the odd personalities. This is schizotypal, schizoid and paranoid. These are more rare. These people are odd, and they call them the odd personalities. The second cluster is a cluster of uninhibited personality types. These people are relatively uninhibited. This would be narcissistic, anti-social, borderline, and hysterical. That's the second cluster. The third cluster is the inhibited personalities, and that's probably the most common. These people are relatively inhibited. The uninhibited people are grandiose, expansive. These people are more circumspect, careful, et cetera. The inhibited personalities, that would be avoidant, obsessive compulsive, and dependent. So those are clustered together. Now, people don't usually cross clusters. It's not like somebody is borderline and obsessive compulsive, because that would imply that they are uninhibited and inhibited at the same time. So you just don't see it. It doesn't happen. Usually the traits are within the cluster. You might see somebody that is avoidant and dependent, et cetera, but ... So that's one of the problems here is that, you know, when we're talking about Mr. Landzo, there are a lot of things that don't make sense. I mean, we are crossing personality clusters, and we get a situation like, on the one hand, we have this information that this is a peaceful -- he was a peaceful boy who was shy and was afraid of goats, okay? And he liked small children and he tried to help others. So we get that information. But then, at the same time, we get the information that he was sort of a semi-thug. It just doesn't make sense. Also, the way he describes it, everything he did at Celebici, and also to a certain extent beyond, was because of Delic. I mean, Delic told him to do all this stuff. In fact, Delic even told him to commit suicide. He couldn't even commit suicide without somebody telling him to or trying to. But on the other hand, he is supposed to be anti-social, which is this cunning and clever person. It just doesn't make sense. The other thing is there's been information presented that he's supposed to be schizoid which means he doesn't like to be around people. He's real odd, and he just doesn't like to be around people at all. On the other hand, he is complaining because he's going back in isolation again, and he won't be around people. So, you know, there's these contradictions and he's supposed to be schizoid, but he's supposed to be narcissistic. He doesn't like to be around people. He's isolated. He's detached from human relations, but he's narcissistic, and that means that he is real grandiose and likes to be on stage. It just doesn't make any sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, given that you don't believe, sort of, all the various psychiatric evaluations of Mr. Landzo have made sense and have been contradictory, can you give us your opinion about what you found concerning whether Mr. Landzo had a personality disorder and whether or not he had certain personality traits, even if he didn't have a disorder, and just explain your own findings a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. See, I didn't find that he had any specific personality disorder. He just didn't meet the criteria. I didn't find he met the criteria for a disorder, but he did have personality traits. My sense of him is his traits are around this cluster sea which is avoidant, dependent, obsessive compulsive. That's the way he comes across. He's a guy that was relatively -- when he was growing up, and I'm not offering this in mitigation because he did have free will, but -- by the way, this kind of constellation of traits, this cluster sea of avoidant, dependent, obsessive compulsive, you often see that. I've seen a lot in Vietnam veterans who have been involved in wartime misbehaviour. I mean, it's not that unusual. There can be considerable underlying anger within this cluster, within this profile. And the anger in his case is because of his sort of chronic passivity and his feelings of impotence and shame. That's something he has always had. He's always been sort of a weakling. You know, he couldn't engage in sports. He had asthma. His big brother dominated him. There's a lot of -- you know, the passivity sort of underlies the anger that eventually came out. I mean, he has a lot of hostility. He is sort of overcontrolled. He tries to look bad at times. He tries to look good. He refuses to take responsibility. He blames others. These are all part of this cluster. These are his traits. I won't go so far, though, as to say that he meets criteria for any disorder. He's along the continuum, but in any of the actual personality disorders in this cluster, I don't think he meets the criteria. But he did -- he does, I'm not saying he's a perfectly normal person. I'm saying that he has problems. But, for the purposes of the Tribunal and for the purposes of what he's charged with, I don't really think it's applicable. I mean, it's just his personality. And I think -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do I take it, then, sir, that you would disagree with the opinion of others if they found he had an anti-social personality disorder, or whether or not he had a schizoid personality disorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, the problem I have with anti-social personality disorder is it's very hard to diagnose that because, well, for two reasons: The main reason, I mean, he was in a war. So, you know, he's going to exhibit some aggressive traits. And what I would like to see, and what you have to see for anti-social personality, is you have to see a conduct disorder prior to age 15. And you know, I know one of the expert witnesses says let's not nit-pick. Well, I mean that's what the criteria are for, we have to nit-pick. And the criteria say that prior to age 15 he has to engage in this kind of behaviour. Well, I have no evidence that he did. What they were talking about, you know, he was with some gangs of boys, that was after he was age 15. What you see in anti-social, you used to see a triad of behaviour which was torturing animals, fire setting and bed wetting. Those are three things that you usually saw in the development in the anti-social personality. When the person was young. He was, he was a friend of animals. I mean, he loved animals. He wasn't -- he should have been torturing the animals, not taking them in. So, I don't -- he just doesn't meet the criteria.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, as part of your evaluation, did Mr. Cowles give you an issue of diminished responsibility coming from English law that has been proposed by Defence counsel for the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he didn't, I mean I found some stuff, I don't know a lot about that, but I found some stuff about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Without for one minute suggesting that definition should be adopted by this Court or even that it will be adopted by this Court, can you just apply that definition to your findings concerning Mr. Landzo and explain that a little bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One thing, apparently it has something to do with the abnormality of the mind. It isn't, you don't have to have a defined psychiatric diagnosis, per se. But an abnormality of the mind, the abnormality of the mind was defined in this 1960 case as a state of mind so different from that of ordinary human beings that the reasonable man would term it abnormal. Well, interacting with Mr. Landzo, I don't know if the reasonable man would term him abnormal. You know, setting aside psychiatric diagnoses, would the reasonable man term this man abnormal?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And thus, do you have an opinion as to whether or not the accused had diminished responsibility in 1992? And would you then please explain your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think he did. I mean, whatever, whatever you invoke, if you invoke PTSD, if you invoke personality disorder, whatever you try to invoke, he still had free will, he still had a choice. We have developed some criteria that link PTSD to criminal behaviour, and it's in my report. And basically, you know, when it's been applicable, it's been an isolated incident where the choice of the victim was accidental, it was unpremeditated, his behaviour was systematic over time. He was systematically -- that's not, that doesn't link. PTSD has nothing to do with it. So I don't think that any of these things we're talking about are, other than the underlying dynamics which make it understandable, at least it's understandable to me, other than that, I don't think diminished responsibility is applicable.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that the personality traits that you indicated Mr. Landzo had are, in fact, not uncommon in large numbers of criminals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are not uncommon, period. I mean, I don't know about criminals, but certainly they are not uncommon in Vietnam veterans who have been involved in, I wouldn't say similar experiences, but wartime misdeeds. In fact, I would like to add they used to recruit people like this for what they called the Phoenix Squadron, they would recruit people like this for that. It was a counter-insurgency, counter-terrorist assassination squadron. They used to recruit people like Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They purposely recruit persons of such traits, recruited to carry out these assignments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wanted anti-authority people, they wanted people with underlying hostility. They wanted smart people, too, so, I don't know if -- but they, you know. One of my best friends is one of the guys that was in this thing, and, yeah, they used to -- and they were young. I mean, they are young, he's malleable, I mean, 18 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have some, but if Mrs. McMurrey wants to go first, I have no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The defence for Mr. Delic has no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate the offer of Mr. Moran, but we are going in the order of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, he is your witness that is being rebutted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, he is a witness for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, but rebutting your own medical evidence.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, if Mr. Moran is going to cross --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you choose, but definitely the evidence about the medical fitness of Landzo is the subject matter of this rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I have plenty of cross-examination for this witness, but the Defence has chosen to follow the order of the indictment, and I will go along with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him do what --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Hi, Dr. Sparr.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: We chatted about two minutes right where you're sitting before we started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You said a couple of things that intrigued me and I would like to follow up on them a little bit. You talked about a stressor about ten months before Celebici. What you had in mind, was the alleged Croatian death camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you have any independent evidence that that thing existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Even if it did exist, he got over it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he got over it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Two other things I want to kind of put together: You said that he's a person who refuses to take responsibility for his own actions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And he blames other people for his wrongs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And then you said he blamed Mr. Delic for these kind of wrongs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did, constant, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: This would be consistent with finding an excuse for one's own actions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And pointing the finger at someone else just to look for some way to take this guilt away from yourself for what you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, it's shame. I mean, he wants to, he doesn't -- he's trying to -- in this particular personality cluster, I mean, people don't like to be criticised, they don't like to take responsibility. The problem is if they don't take responsibility, then they, they feel passive and impotent. So they are caught; on one hand they don't want to responsibility because they are afraid to be criticised or make a mistake; but on the other hand, if they don't take responsibility, then they are passive and feel impotent and feel anger and hostility. So, I mean, he's in the impotent passive kind of --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: This is kind of consistent with, for instance, you saw in the reports that he blamed his father for him not being able to go to art school.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, he's always blaming people. Until he takes responsibility, I mean, he just doesn't take responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, for instance, it wasn't his dad's fault he couldn't go to art school, but he blames his father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Even though his father is not at fault for anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And the other thing that you said that was kind of intriguing to me, and I'd like to just follow it up just a bit is this: You said that when the personality disorder, the clusters, he is kind of all over the place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, he's been put all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, did you find that there was evidence that he was all over the place, if you would?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't, no, I don't think so. To me he's not all over the place. He's a pretty inhibited guy, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Again, having read some of the reports from Lagazzi and some of the others, with the attempts of manipulating the system, would that be consistent with what you found to take this blame away from himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's trying to deflect criticism and he will lie to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Convincingly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how convincingly it is. I don't -- it's not that convincing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: But it is, he will lie to deflect this criticism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Out of the whole cloth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Out of the what?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Whole cloth. Just have nothing to do with reality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He has a goal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What's his goal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His goal is to deflect criticism, but I don't, you know, I don't think he just lies to lie, just because he likes to lie. I think he doesn't like to get caught.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And so, he will lie to avoid blame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Pass the witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Sparr.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We have met before, we met when you came to interview Mr. Landzo a couple of weeks ago, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, for 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Right, we never discussed this case or your evaluation of Mr. Landzo before, have we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you went to see Mr. Landzo, I believe, the day that I ran into you, it was about seven o'clock p.m. in the lobby of the Bel Air Hotel, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, approximately, right, because I saw him, both times I saw him was like 7 to 8.30.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, if the records at the detention centre said you were there for an hour and 15 minutes on that day and one hour the next day; would they be incorrect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I thought I was there longer. Maybe that's because he is obsessive or something, but I thought I was there longer. My sense was I was there an hour and a half. It seemed longer, I don't know. I'm sure they are correct.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you say he's obsessive, are you referring to this hour and 15 minute and one hour that I have just cited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm referring to the fact that he gives a lot of detail, elaborates quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sparr, I mean Dr. Sparr, excuse me, I know that you were hired, in fact in your report, your report states that you were contacted by Mr. Cowles of the office of the Prosecutor and asked to evaluate Mr. Landzo particularly in regard to the presence or absence of a psychiatric condition known as Post Traumatic Stress Disorder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And your examination could hardly be considered neutral when your sole purpose was to look for the presence or absence of PTSD; wouldn't that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand, why. I mean, its presence or absence. So --

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Right, but you weren't there to evaluate him and look for, to completely evaluate him as far as his mental condition; you were there to look for the presence or absence of one condition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there to do a psychiatric evaluation. We're focusing on PTSD because that was the focus of the reports I saw previously. But I was basically there to do a psychiatric evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But your report says that you were there to look for the presence or absence of PTSD, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says particularly.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Particularly in regard to the presence or absence of PTSD.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you just referred to those prior reports which did refer to PTSD, but that's not the sole diagnosis of those reports, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, you say you specialise in general psychiatry, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And so, you are not representing to this Court that you're a forensic psychiatrist, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you know the difference in a forensic psychiatrist and general psychiatry, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a forensic psychiatrist takes a three-hour multiple choice exam, and if a person -- excuse me, a general psychiatrist takes a three-hour multiple choice exam, and if that person passes the exam, they can say that they have added qualification in forensic psychiatry. Nobody ever watches them interview a patient or anything, it's a multiple choice exam.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So, you don't give much credence to people who claim to specialise in forensic psychiatry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I give them a lot of credence. I said that's the process for being a forensic psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is that the process in Oregon or is that the process --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the process in the US

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And so being a forensic psychiatrist doesn't have anything to do with your experience in evaluating people and applying it to the criminal or legal systems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, not, not before you take the exam. Once you take the exam the assumption is that you will be engaged in forensic psychiatry. You know, I suppose some people are and some people aren't.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But the main difference between you and a forensic psychiatrist is a forensic psychiatrist passed a three-hour multiple choice test?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, you deal mainly with veterans as the chief of psychiatry at the Department of Veterans Affairs Medical Centre in Portland Oregon, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, you've written numerous articles discrediting the claims of PTSD on veterans involved in the Vietnam War, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The focus of the articles is to be careful when you evaluate people and, you know, PTSD or whatever, and use the criteria.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And are you talking about the criteria that you have cited in your report, which is a three-step criteria, or are you referring to the criteria under DSM-IV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: DSM-IV.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Which is a seven-step criteria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In DSM-IV there is three, three clusters. There's avoidance, re-experiencing and arousal.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But those are not the only criteria.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, under each one there are several.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Right. But in your report you only listed three, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, I listed the main.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution has introduced into evidence P264 and I just want to go to your CV that is now in evidence. And I happen to have read one of the articles you listed on there, it was the only one I had access to. But there's an article where you call it a mine field, and you talk about PTSD and expert testimony in the field of torts. Do you know what article I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And in that article --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Post Traumatic Stress Disorder in Tort Actions, Forensic Mine Field.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Right, that's the article. And in that article you basically have accumulated other doctors' opinions as far as DSM-IV, and then you have said that expert testimony should not be relied upon; isn't that what you said in that article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That expert testimony should not be relied upon? Actually I haven't seen the article in a long time, so you're going to have to quote Sparr to Sparr, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I have a copy of the article if it would refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher I would like to provide Dr. Sparr a copy of his article.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D90/4.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, in that report, isn't it mainly an accumulation of other doctors' opinions as far as DSM-IV goes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall that, but -- where are you?

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think the highlighted parts would show you the doctors.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Isn't it mainly an accumulation of other doctors' opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if I would characterise it that way. You're looking at page 290, is that what you're --

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately I don't have another copy of the article in front of me, but it's highlighted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm basically referencing other opinions.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And isn't it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Isn't it true that in that report you say that expert testimony with regard to personality disorders and anxiety disorders should not be offered in the courtroom? Isn't that basically what you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let's see. Can you point to where that --

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, but Dr. Sparr, you wrote that article, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And it's one that's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually I wrote this article ten years ago. So, I mean --

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But it is one listed on your CV for your accreditation, and everything, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think she's arguing with the witness. She asked him a question, he asked her to point out the section to which she's referring to, and I believe if she wants to ask him a question about a specific conclusion, she should be able, she should show him that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: She is not, she is merely referring to his opinion in that article which he now says was an opinion which might have been expressed ten years ago. This is what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if, I'm trying to -- I'm not trying to be difficult, but I'm trying to figure out what -- I mean this sort of -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Dr. Sparr. Anyway, you wrote that article and it expresses your opinion with regard to DSM-IV and expert testimony; and is that correct, Dr. Sparr?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'd like to offer that article into evidence as, to show his tendency and bias in this field of DSM-IV and expert testimony. And he has verified that he wrote it. I would like the Court to accept it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still don't understand how it's -- I mean, somehow the way you're characterising it is not resonating with me, so, I don't know. I mean, you're.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Sparr --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm trying to find where you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Counsel is only suggesting that you in past gave such opinions from ideas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I've got nothing against expert opinion or anything. I mean, it's just not, I mean, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Dr. Sparr and I believe now that it's in evidence the Court can draw their own conclusions. So I will move onto another subject. Actually, I do want to cover this. This is in relation to tort actions in the United States; isn't it, this article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, this article, right, correct.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you do know the difference between the standard and burden of proof in tort actions and a forensic application to criminal cases, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Just one second. I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, it appears from your report that you applied a test in your report which you claim was developed to validate a link between PTSD and the criminal act in question; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And that test that you have written about is AS - blank in 1985, blank being a name, not that I forgot it, and it was applied in the trauma of war: Stress and Recovery in Vietnam vets; isn't that what you applied here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Let's just take a look. Let's say -- by the way, by the way, Dr. Sparr, are you familiar with this book by Kaplan and Sadok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The Synopsis of Psychiatry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is this a well-known authority in the psychiatric field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And do almost every psychiatrist, even internationally, rely upon this book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about internationally, but people have it. I mean, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Do you have this book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And if I were to tell you that nowhere in this book is there a mention of this blank test, AS - blank test relating PTSD to criminal activity, would you believe me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, that test, I want to take your report, if you don't mind. Do you have your report right there in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 3 of your report where you refer to this test.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And on page 3, don't you, I mean, assuming this is a valid test, even if we were assuming this is a valid test, I would like to take each one of these one through nine and discuss them with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In order to develop a link between PTSD and the criminal act in question: Number one, the act represents spontaneous unpremeditated behaviour, uncharacteristic of the individual. Now, that could absolutely fit Mr. Landzo; couldn't it, as far as 1992, which you've read about him in the Celebici camp? He was not violent before, he was a timid boy, he was quiet, he was sickly; so that could possibly fit him, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time he did it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, number two, coherent dialogue, appropriately related to time and place is lacking. Now, you read all of these statements, all of the different statements, all of the contradictory evaluations, all of the, not contradictory evaluations, but all the relations of Mr. Landzo. Now coherent dialogue appropriately related to time and place is lacking; that could apply to Mr. Landzo, too, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so. I mean, what that is saying is that basically the person thinks they are somewhere else. So, they are not, I mean, if they are instructing somebody to do something, it shouldn't make any sense. I mean, what they are doing shouldn't make any sense to that person because they think they are somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Sparr, of course, we don't have anything to base this questioning on, because you only have it as a footnote. But what you're relating to is more of a psychosis than PTSD, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about a disassociative state, where a person is -- I mean, they think they are somewhere else, and they are acting as if they are in a combat situation or some situation that requires violence or something, which in fact it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on to number 3. The choice of victim is fortuitous and accidental, you read in some of your reports that these people he didn't think of as human beings, they were thought of things that had to be dealt with. So couldn't Mr. Landzo fit under the category of number 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't really see how, because, I mean, he knew who the victim was, so, I mean it's not like he's going to get somebody, he's calling them out.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You don't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's not randomly -- you know, he's got specific people in mind.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, so you're discounting the fact that he was following orders, in several of the reports it says these people no longer were human beings to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm saying that he's looking for specific people, and that he's not just indiscriminately finding somebody -- I mean, the orders part of it is not part of this, but I'm just saying that his choice of a victim is not fortuitous or accidental.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Let's go on to number 4, the response is disproportionate to the provocation. Surely you can't say that did not exist in Mr. Landzo, even if you were to evaluate him from 1996 and go back to the injuring of his hand in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And number five, the act is rationally inexplicable and lacks current motivation; that can apply to Mr. Landzo, too, can't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, it could.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And number six, the act recreates in a psychologically meaningful way elements of the original traumatic stressor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And I think that one is absolutely key. The stressor was violence, and now what is he doing? Is he recreating that same thing? Isn't that child abuse? If you were an abused child, you're more likely to be a child abuser as you get older? Isn't that the same kind of a premise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not abused.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm just talking about the stressor being a violent act, in Celebici he was recreating another violent act. That can apply to him, too, can't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you talking about the stressor in the camp, the supposed camp?

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The stressor in the camp, I mean, he was not in danger himself. He was a spectator, so ...

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Sparr. Number 7: "The defendant is unaware of the ways in which he has re-enacted traumatic experiences." Mr. Landzo didn't tell you, "I was re-enacting that Croatian camp every time I beat somebody at Celebici"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Number 8: "The act is precipitated by events or circumstances that realistically or symbolically force the individual to face unresolved conflicts." That applies to Mr. Landzo too, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I would have to think about that. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Let's go on to number 9, the last one: "There is amnesia for the episode." I don't know if you read all the reports, but if you did, you would know that in 1996 he was unable to remember every event which he did remember later after therapy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Despite the passage of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, the passage of time, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's probably true, that he -- I'm not sure the reason is because of PTSD. I mean, I won't say that it isn't, but he probably -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Sparr. In your evaluation of PTSD, have you had an opportunity to look at Defence Exhibit 81/4, Defence Exhibit 82/4 and Defence Exhibit 48/4? I'll just tell you what they are, because I'm sure you've had them. One is Dr. Gripon's summary of PTSD and the personality disorders that was introduced into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I briefly looked at that.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And D82/4 is a grid which has the different names for the ICD-10, the DSM-3R and the DSM-IV. Have you had a chance to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen that.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And D48/4 is a diagnostic criteria from DSM-IV on the personality disorders. I'm sure you're familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. When you looked at your three basic tenets of PTSD, the traumatic event -- just one second. I need to find my book. You say, "The traumatic event is persistently re-experienced. 2) Persistent avoidance of the stimuli associated with the trauma and the numbing of general responsiveness. 3) persistent symptoms of increased arousal." I'm sorry. There's a D47/4 which is the criteria for PTSD. Do you have that in front of you? I mean, not that, but if you have it in your book, I'm sure it's the same diagnostic criteria. It's one that looks like this but it says "PTSD" on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the diagnostic criteria.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. In the diagnostic criteria for PTSD, you claimed that he didn't fit any of the symptoms for PTSD, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that he didn't fit any of the symptoms. I said he didn't fit -- this is when I interviewed him last or this month, actually.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You just stated that he was not suffering from PTSD in 1992, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't think so.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go through this a little bit. Of course, "A," he was or was not exposed to a traumatic event, but assuming that he was, that fits "A" under DSM-IV, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm assuming that he did experience that the way he describes it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Let's go into that detail a little bit more. There's something known as the zone of danger, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: What is the zone of danger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that means that somebody is in -- they could potentially be in harm's way. In other words, they are within an area where there is something going on that is adverse, and they are within striking distance.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In PTSD, the zone of danger is not just one occurrence. It can be a continuing experience if you feel like you are still existing in that zone of danger, can't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on to "B." "The traumatic event is persistently re-experienced in one or more of the following ways," and there's five listed there, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I really don't want to read each one to the Court, but can you yourself just pick out a couple where you think Mr. Landzo might fit under, 1 through 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When are you talking about? Are you talking about now or --

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm talking about after your review of all the reports in 1992. "Recurrent and intrusive distressing recollections of the event." He had to take sleeping pills to sleep, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure that he did. That pills thing, I'm not sure when he took them, when he didn't take them. That's -- the information about that is very erratic. I'm not sure. I don't know if he was taking it right after he came back from the camp. I sort of recall -- I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. "Recurrent distressing dreams of the event." Now, that has been rampant in every one of the reports, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure in '92. I think that he was probably experiencing some of this for awhile, but it appears that it went away.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And it appears that it went away when, Dr. Sparr?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly before he got to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So the reports that you did didn't have that he was suffering from recurrent dreams over here in the U.N. detention centre in 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's '96.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. That would be after --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We're talking about '92.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: See, I'm not saying that he wasn't affected by this orientation camp. I'm just saying that I'm not sure the effect lasted that long.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Number 3, did I already say number 3, acting or feeling as if the traumatic event were recurring. I think I already covered that. Number 4, "Intense psychological distress at exposure to internal or external cues that symbolise or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event." Now, distress is expressed in many different ways, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Number 5, "Physiologic reactivity on exposure to internal or external cues." Now, physiologic reactivity can be recreating, can't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, a physiologic response can be startle, high heart rate, you know, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Let's go to number "C" and about the avoidance issue. Your statement is that because he went directly into the Territorial Defence and asked to be sent to the front-line, that he was not experiencing avoidance of the issue; isn't that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Avoidance can come in many different ways, can't it? In fact, the precursor here that it can also be a general numbing of responsiveness, can't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You do remember in the reports that he no longer even saw people as human beings; don't you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yeah, but, see, at the same time, I mean, he was trying to help people. I don't know if you can go that far that he didn't see people as human beings. I think there was some numbing when he originally came back from the orientation camp, but once again, it went away. I mean, I'm saying that he experienced an acute stress reaction from that experience but that it subsided.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that he did not develop chronic PTSD from that experience.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Let's just go on to C-4, "Markedly diminished interest or participation in significant activities." After the Celebici camp, did you read the testimony of the people who said that he was there but he was alone, that he didn't participate or hang out with other people, that he stayed by himself only with his dogs? Did you read that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But he also joined the military police. He started relationships with two women.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That's another thing I want to ask you. Does a relationship with a woman mean that he doesn't have PTSD?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on to number 5, "Feeling of detachment or estrangement from others." Under letter "C," it says you only have to have three or more of the following. We've already gotten to five. We already have five, but let's go on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know we've gone through the five, but I'm not saying that he had all of those things.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I understand that. You're not saying that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Number 5, "Feeling of detachment or estrangement from others." Did you get that from the reports that were written by everybody else and the evidence that you've seen and the testimony that you've read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had that at times but, you know, at times he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Let's go on to number 6. "Restricted range of affect. Unable to have loving feelings." Did every one of these people say that they thought he was detached and cold and unable to express his emotions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were talking about their evaluation of him now, you know, when they saw him, whenever they evaluated him, '96, '97. And that was their opinion.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Let's just go on to number 7. "A sense of foreshortened future. Does not expect to have a career, marriage, children, or a normal life span." Would you say that trying to commit suicide in 1994 and 1996 and asking for a firing squad, would that indicate that he has a foreshortened future, that he only sees a foreshortened future?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At times, he has had a foreshorted future. Also, the suicide attempts are more like suicide gestures rather than attempts. I mean, he has had that feeling. When I interviewed him this month, he did not have a foreshortened future, and my question has always been if he had PTSD, what happened to it?

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Sparr, are you saying in July of 1998 when you interviewed Mr. Landzo that if he had therapy and 18 months of trying to overcome this condition, that he didn't have it 18 months before or four years before or five years before? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm -- no, I'm not saying that necessarily. I don't know about 1996. I'm more sure of 1992 and 1998. I'm not sure about 1996. I know he was depressed in 1996. There are certainly some things that are consistent with PTSD in 1996 specifically. I'm not saying that he won't again develop PTSD. In fact, I would expect him to develop PTSD. I don't think he had it in '92. He certainly doesn't have it now. He could have had it in '96. And I think he probably will, once he starts taking responsibility, I think he will develop symptoms again.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Sparr, you just said you're absolutely sure he did not have PTSD in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me qualify that.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That's after your evaluation for two hours at the U.N. detention centre that you've come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I read all the other reports too.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: All the other reports say he had PTSD, don't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they don't. They don't all say he had PTSD.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In 1996, they all say he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think they all do. No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Let's go on to "D." "Persistent symptoms of increased arousal." This only has to be indicated by two or more of the following. Number 1, "Difficulty falling or staying asleep." He could fit under that category, couldn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the way, a lot of these symptoms, in fact, most of them, are also associated with depression.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Right, but we're going through the criteria right now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know, but they are also associated with depression.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you just told me that you can't jump axis, that you can't have one from one cluster and one from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Depression is an Axis I.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Right, and this is Axis II.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you can certainly, certainly have Axis I and Axis II diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm glad you clarified that for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Number 2 under "D": "Irritability or outbursts of anger." Now, in 1992, you have to admit that Mr. Landzo, in all psychiatric probability, did experience that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's part of his personality.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Number 3 -- well, I don't know about difficulty concentrating. Number 5: "Exaggerated startled response." I guess we cannot go to those. But out of all of these that you've seen, he certainly could, in psychiatric probability terms, have fit into three or more of "C" and two or more of "D," couldn't he have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in '92 or '98, as far as I'm concerned. Possibly in '96.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Sparr, I will absolutely agree with your diagnosis in 1998. I do not believe that Mr. Landzo is suffering from PTSD at this time. But I wanted to ask you about how you're absolutely positive he was not suffering from PTSD in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has given his reasons so many times.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's just because of his behaviour. It's just not consistent with PTSD. It's because of his behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe you said that the stressor that was described, he probably just got over it quickly. Now, you're not saying that having someone brutally murdered in front of you when you're 18 years old, because he didn't participate in it, that that stressor was not valid under PTSD, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. I have to find your report that I have here. Now, in your report, the bottom of page 3, you say: "When I first interviewed Mr. Landzo on July 6, 1998, it was immediately apparent that he now does not have PTSD"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, how was that immediately apparent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because of the next sentence. He was so -- you know, he was so optimistic and he was kind of -- I mean, he was hopeful. He was looking for the future.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But being hopeful and looking for the future doesn't mean that they have PTSD at that time. It's just one of the criteria, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's just one of the criteria, but people with PTSD, they are just not hopeful. They are just not, so ...

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, you're saying that he wasn't suffering PTSD because he wasn't avoidant at the U.N. detention centre. What is it that he was supposed to be avoiding at the U.N. detention centre? That is at the top of page 4. "Rather than avoidant, he was actively engaged in his current situation." What was he supposed to be avoiding at the U.N. detention centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I was saying, you know, just like avoiding the trial and not -- you know, not participating. I mean, he was like another -- as Dr. Lagazzi said, he was like another attorney or something.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is that what you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You referred to that as "hyper-adjusted"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And hyper-adjusted could be another avoidance mechanism, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, you know, he's trying to look good and competent and proactive. I mean, he likes that. He's not being passive.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But my question was: Hyper-adjusted could be another avoidance mechanism, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Avoidance of what?

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was asking you. You're saying he was avoiding the trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But you're the one that's saying it's an avoidance mechanism.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You said in 1998 he did not have PTSD, but you're claiming that he was engaged in activity that showed that he was not avoidant. You said something about avoiding the trial. Is that something he would be avoiding if he were suffering from PTSD at the U.N. detention centre in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He certainly could be, sure. I mean, if he wasn't hopeful, yeah. I mean, I don't think he would be that involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a couple more pages here. I was wondering if it might be appropriate to take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will break and come back at noon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Proceed, Mrs. McMurrey.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Sparr, I want to go back to your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And I think Mrs. McHenry's question was, you were here to answer the issues of the mental health of the accused; isn't that what Mrs. McHenry asked you? And you said yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you were really here to determine PTSD, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, I already answered that. I mean.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You're right, you have answered it. Now, you also said in your direct examination you determined that he didn't have PTSD because of the way he interacts with others. Now, you didn't see how he interacted with others in 1992, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you talked about personality disorders as the end of a continuum, that all people have personality disorders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that, I said personality traits, personality traits.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Personality traits of the listing of the criteria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But the difference between DSM-IV and personality traits and personality disorders would be that personality disorders are pervasive in a personality and excessive; wouldn't that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And they cause symptoms. In other words, the person is suffering in some respects. They cause symptoms. They cause dysphoria.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Could you explain what dysphoria is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means feeling bad.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And all personality disorders cause dysphoria; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them do eventually. Not all the time, but eventually, yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, people with severe personality disorders might not recognise that they are feeling bad, would they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They might not for a time.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, you also stated in your direct examination that there was no crossing of the clusters. And then on cross-examination you said, oh, you didn't mean there was no crossing of the clusters. So, which one is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, you were talking about Axis I versus Axis II. And, I mean, those are different axis; so, you know, there can be diagnosis in Axis I and Axis II.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Axis II there is -- I'm not familiar with any crossing of the clusters. I mean, I suppose it's possible, but not in my experience.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCMURREY
